item.title: RHOPE Framework Uses LLM Proxies for Bayesian Adaptive Experimentation
item.description:
RHOPE Framework Uses LLM Proxies for Bayesian Adaptive Experimentation

A new research framework called Residual Horizon Optimization for Prediction-Powered Experimentation (RHOPE) has been introduced. This approach combines large language models (LLMs) with Bayesian adaptive experimentation to improve the allocation of measurement efforts across candidate treatments. The method was submitted on November 25, 2026.

🔍 Overview

The core challenge addressed is the allocation of limited measurement effort across candidate treatments to learn their expected outcomes. While adaptive designs refine allocations as evidence accumulates to improve estimation and treatment selection, exploiting unstructured or high-dimensional context remains a difficult task. The researchers propose using LLMs to transform this complex context into proxy outcomes, allowing for more informed decision-making during experimentation.

🧩 How it works

RHOPE is a principled Bayesian adaptive experimentation framework that integrates true outcomes with LLM-generated proxy outcomes. It formulates finite-batch design as a posterior Markov decision process (MDP). The methodology utilizes proxy outcomes in two distinct ways:

  • Sample augmentation: Improves estimation precision.
  • Advance information: Observing proxies before each allocation decision provides prior information for decision-making.

⚙️ Key details

Testing of the methodology has been conducted on synthetic experiments and semi-synthetic experiments using Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) data. These experiments suggest that estimation precision drives most of the gains, with smaller additional benefits coming from advance information. The results highlight the importance of proxy informativeness and moment-estimation accuracy in the framework’s performance.

#LLMs #BayesianAdaptation #ExperimentalDesign #RHOPE

Source: RHOPE: LLM-Augmented Adaptive Experimental Design with Complex Contextual Information

item.title: New Method Uses Quantization Error for High-Dimensional Space-Filling Designs
item.description:
New Method Uses Quantization Error for High-Dimensional Space-Filling Designs

Researchers propose a new approach to space-filling design in computer experiments that replaces traditional maximin and minimax criteria with quantization error of the uniform measure on a hypercube, addressing sensitivity to boundaries and high-dimensional limitations.

🔍 Overview

  • Maximin and minimax criteria suffer major drawbacks in high dimensions.
  • Deploying space-filling designs requires extremely large numbers of design points when dimension $d$ is very large.
  • These criteria are highly sensitive to boundaries, especially vertices of a hypercube, particularly when design size is less than $2^d$.

🧩 How it works

  • Uses quantization error of the uniform measure on the hypercube instead of maximin or minimax criteria.
  • Quantization error accounts for the entire distribution of distances from a random point to the design.
  • It is less sensitive to boundary effects than maximin and minimax criteria.
  • Zador’s theorem enables a smooth transition to uniform designs as design size tends to infinity.
  • Builds on recent results on optimal random quantizers for spherically symmetric distributions (arXiv:2610.11772).
  • Generates random designs of target size $n$ with small $L_s$-mean quantization error.
  • The support of the resulting distribution constructs designs, possibly incrementally, with sizes up to $n$.

⚙️ Key details

  • Designs supported on a fractional factorial subset of the vertices of a small hypercube perform exceptionally well for moderate $n$.
  • These designs perform significantly better than designs uniformly distributed over the entire hypercube.
  • The method explains how to account for projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces.

💡 Why it matters

  • Addresses the fundamental limitation of traditional space-filling criteria in high dimensions.
  • Provides a less boundary-sensitive alternative that scales naturally with design size.
  • Demonstrates practical construction using fractional factorial subsets of vertices, offering computational advantages.

#SpaceFillingDesign #QuantizationError #HighDimensions #ComputerExperiments #OptimalQuantizers

Source: Sparse designs via quantization of the uniform measure on high-dimensional hypercubes
